claim: The inferior parietal lobule (IPL) is one of the most expanded cortical regions in humans relative to other primates.
source: The inferior parietal lobule (IPL) is one of the most expanded cortical regions in humans relative to other primates.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Orban et al., 2006; Van Essen and Dierker, 2007; Kaas, 2012; Ardesch et al., 2019) and established scientific knowledge about primate brain evolution.

claim: The IPL is among the most structurally and functionally asymmetric regions in the human cerebral cortex.
source: It is also among the most structurally and functionally asymmetric regions in the human cerebral cortex.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: IPL subregions exhibited positive allometric scaling in both hemispheres across rhesus macaque monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans.
source: We identified IPL subregions that exhibited positive allometric in both hemispheres, scaling across rhesus macaque monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A showing allometric scaling relationships.

claim: The patterns of IPL subregions asymmetry were similar in chimpanzees and humans.
source: The patterns of IPL subregions asymmetry were similar in chimpanzees and humans, but no IPL asymmetries were evident in macaques.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B showing volumetric asymmetries.

claim: No IPL asymmetries were evident in macaques.
source: The patterns of IPL subregions asymmetry were similar in chimpanzees and humans, but no IPL asymmetries were evident in macaques.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B showing no significant asymmetries in macaques.

claim: Humans showed the most widespread asymmetric connections in the frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices among the comparative sample of primates.
source: Among the comparative sample of primates, humans showed the most widespread asymmetric connections in the frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, constituting leftward asymmetric networks that may provide an anatomical basis for language and tool use.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4 showing connectivity asymmetries.

claim: Leftward asymmetric networks in humans may provide an anatomical basis for language and tool use.
source: Among the comparative sample of primates, humans showed the most widespread asymmetric connections in the frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, constituting leftward asymmetric networks that may provide an anatomical basis for language and tool use.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed connectivity patterns and their relationship to known functional specializations.

claim: Unique human asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and primary motor cortex might be related to handedness.
source: Unique human asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and primary motor cortex might be related to handedness.
evidence: Based on speculation about the functional significance of observed connectivity patterns.

claim: Structural and connectional asymmetries may underlie hemispheric specialization of the human brain.
source: These findings suggest that structural and connectional asymmetries may underlie hemispheric specialization of the human brain.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined structural and connectivity findings.

claim: The association cortex has expanded greatly in size in human brain evolution.
source: The association cortex has expanded greatly in size and exhibits modified connectivity patterns in human brain evolution (Orban et al., 2006; Mars et al., 2017; Ardesch et al., 2019; Van Essen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The association cortex exhibits modified connectivity patterns in human brain evolution.
source: The association cortex has expanded greatly in size and exhibits modified connectivity patterns in human brain evolution (Orban et al., 2006; Mars et al., 2017; Ardesch et al., 2019; Van Essen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The association cortex displays disproportionate expansion in conjunction with overall neocortical volume enlargement across primates.
source: Compared with the primary sensory and motor cortical regions, the association cortex displays disproportionate expansion in conjunction with overall neocortical volume enlargement across primates (Chaplin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Association areas comprise a large percentage of the neocortex in human brains.
source: Accordingly, association areas comprise a large percentage of the neocortex in human brains (Orban et al., 2006; Van Essen and Dierker, 2007; Donahue et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Functional and neuroanatomical asymmetries are more extreme in humans compared with other primate species, especially in the association cortex.
source: Functional and neuroanatomical asymmetries are also pronounced in the human brain, appearing to be more extreme compared with other primate species, especially in the association cortex (Chance and Crow, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cerebral asymmetry exists not only in humans but also in nonhuman primates.
source: Nevertheless, cerebral asymmetry exists not only in humans but also in nonhuman primates (Gómez-Robles et al., 1761; Hopkins, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Olive baboons and chimpanzees showed population-level leftward volumetric asymmetry in the planum temporale.
source: For example, olive baboons and chimpanzees showed population-level leftward volumetric asymmetry in the planum temporale, which is thought to be homologous to part of Wernicke's area in humans and may have played a facilitating role in the evolution of spoken language (Spocter et al., 2010; Marie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The planum temporale is thought to be homologous to part of Wernicke's area in humans.
source: For example, olive baboons and chimpanzees showed population-level leftward volumetric asymmetry in the planum temporale, which is thought to be homologous to part of Wernicke's area in humans and may have played a facilitating role in the evolution of spoken language (Spocter et al., 2010; Marie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The planum temporale may have played a facilitating role in the evolution of spoken language.
source: For example, olive baboons and chimpanzees showed population-level leftward volumetric asymmetry in the planum temporale, which is thought to be homologous to part of Wernicke's area in humans and may have played a facilitating role in the evolution of spoken language (Spocter et al., 2010; Marie et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Language and complex tool use show considerable lateralization in the human brain.
source: Language and complex tool use, which show considerable lateralization in the human brain, are considered to be universal features of humans (Johnson-Frey et al., 2005; Lewis, 2006; Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Language and complex tool use are considered to be universal features of humans.
source: Language and complex tool use, which show considerable lateralization in the human brain, are considered to be universal features of humans (Johnson-Frey et al., 2005; Lewis, 2006; Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Language and complex tool use both involve the inferior parietal lobule.
source: These specialized functions all involve the inferior parietal lobule (IPL), an area of the association cortex that represents a zone of topographical convergence in the brain (Johnson-Frey, 2004; Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IPL is an area of the association cortex that represents a zone of topographical convergence in the brain.
source: These specialized functions all involve the inferior parietal lobule (IPL), an area of the association cortex that represents a zone of topographical convergence in the brain (Johnson-Frey, 2004; Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IPL is one of the most expanded regions in humans compared with nonhuman primates.
source: Moreover, the IPL is one of the most expanded regions in humans compared with nonhuman primates (Orban et al., 2006; Van Essen and Dierker, 2007; Kaas, 2012; Ardesch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The functional diversity and expansion of the IPL imply that it contains subdivisions that may have been elaborated or developed in the ancestors of modern humans.
source: The functional diversity and expansion of the IPL imply that it contains subdivisions that may have been elaborated or developed in the ancestors of modern humans, allowing new abilities such as extensive tool use and communication using gestures (Kaas, 2012).
evidence: Based on inference from observed characteristics and citation to prior research.

claim: IPL subdivisions may have allowed new abilities such as extensive tool use and communication using gestures.
source: The functional diversity and expansion of the IPL imply that it contains subdivisions that may have been elaborated or developed in the ancestors of modern humans, allowing new abilities such as extensive tool use and communication using gestures (Kaas, 2012).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cellular microstructure alone is insufficient to completely represent brain organization, especially long-range connections.
source: Although the IPL has been subdivided into distinct subregions using cytoarchitecture and this technique has provided invaluable information, cellular microstructure alone is insufficient to completely represent brain organization, especially long-range connections, which are the major determinant of regional specialization (Passingham et al., 2002; Caspers et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Long-range connections are the major determinant of regional specialization.
source: Although the IPL has been subdivided into distinct subregions using cytoarchitecture and this technique has provided invaluable information, cellular microstructure alone is insufficient to completely represent brain organization, especially long-range connections, which are the major determinant of regional specialization (Passingham et al., 2002; Caspers et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Connectivity-based parcellation was successfully used to characterize IPL subdivisions in different species and to perform cross-species comparisons.
source: In previous studies, this technique was successfully used to characterize IPL subdivisions in different species as well as to perform cross-species comparisons (Mars et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The functions and interactions of brain regions are determined by their anatomical connections.
source: The functions and interactions of brain regions are determined by their anatomical connections (Passingham et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: A four-cluster solution revealed a rostral–caudal topological pattern consistent with previous parcellations based on cytoarchitecture and anatomical connectivity.
source: The four-cluster solution revealed a rostral–caudal topological pattern that was consistent with previous parcellations based on cytoarchitecture and anatomical connectivity (Pandya and Seltzer, 1982; Caspers et al., 2006; Mars et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data from the current study and citations to prior research.

claim: The cytoarchitectural definition of macaques revealed four subregions in the IPL.
source: Also, the cytoarchitectural definition of macaques revealed four subregions in the IPL (Pandya and Seltzer, 1982), which was fewer than the seven cytoarchitectural subregions of the human IPL (Caspers et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The human IPL has seven cytoarchitectural subregions.
source: Also, the cytoarchitectural definition of macaques revealed four subregions in the IPL (Pandya and Seltzer, 1982), which was fewer than the seven cytoarchitectural subregions of the human IPL (Caspers et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The IPL contains two major cytoarchitectural divisions across species, the anterior (PF) and posterior (PG) areas.
source: It is widely accepted that the IPL contains two major cytoarchitectural divisions across species, the anterior (PF) and posterior (PG) areas (von Economo and Koskinas, 1925; Von Bonin and Bailey, 1947; Bailey et al., 1950).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: The rostral anterior cluster (C1) is similar to the PFt and part of the PFop area defined using cytoarchitecture.
source: Specifically, the rostral anterior cluster (C1) is similar to the PFt and part of the PFop area defined using cytoarchitecture by Caspers et al., 2006, the caudal anterior cluster (C2) corresponds to the PF and PFm areas, the rostral posterior cluster (C3) is similar to the PGa area, and the caudal posterior cluster (C4) is similar to the PGp area.
evidence: Based on comparison with prior cytoarchitectural definitions cited in the text.

claim: The caudal anterior cluster (C2) corresponds to the PF and PFm areas.
source: Specifically, the rostral anterior cluster (C1) is similar to the PFt and part of the PFop area defined using cytoarchitecture by Caspers et al., 2006, the caudal anterior cluster (C2) corresponds to the PF and PFm areas, the rostral posterior cluster (C3) is similar to the PGa area, and the caudal posterior cluster (C4) is similar to the PGp area.
evidence: Based on comparison with prior cytoarchitectural definitions cited in the text.

claim: The rostral posterior cluster (C3) is similar to the PGa area.
source: Specifically, the rostral anterior cluster (C1) is similar to the PFt and part of the PFop area defined using cytoarchitecture by Caspers et al., 2006, the caudal anterior cluster (C2) corresponds to the PF and PFm areas, the rostral posterior cluster (C3) is similar to the PGa area, and the caudal posterior cluster (C4) is similar to the PGp area.
evidence: Based on comparison with prior cytoarchitectural definitions cited in the text.

claim: The caudal posterior cluster (C4) is similar to the PGp area.
source: Specifically, the rostral anterior cluster (C1) is similar to the PFt and part of the PFop area defined using cytoarchitecture by Caspers et al., 2006, the caudal anterior cluster (C2) corresponds to the PF and PFm areas, the rostral posterior cluster (C3) is similar to the PGa area, and the caudal posterior cluster (C4) is similar to the PGp area.
evidence: Based on comparison with prior cytoarchitectural definitions cited in the text.

claim: The term 'tool' showed a much higher correlation with the left C1 than with the right C1.
source: The term tool showed a much higher correlation with the left C1 than with the right C1, suggesting that the left C1 is more involved in tool use.
evidence: Supported by data from functional decoding analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The left C1 is more involved in tool use.
source: The term tool showed a much higher correlation with the left C1 than with the right C1, suggesting that the left C1 is more involved in tool use.
evidence: Based on inference from functional decoding data.

claim: The left C2 is more involved in tool use and language.
source: Terms such as tool and semantics showed relatively high correlations with the left C2, whereas terms such as nogo and inhibition showed relatively high correlations with the right C2, suggesting that the left C2 is more involved in tool use and language, whereas the right C2 is more involved in executive function.
evidence: Based on inference from functional decoding data.

claim: The right C2 is more involved in executive function.
source: Terms such as tool and semantics showed relatively high correlations with the left C2, whereas terms such as nogo and inhibition showed relatively high correlations with the right C2, suggesting that the left C2 is more involved in tool use and language, whereas the right C2 is more involved in executive function.
evidence: Based on inference from functional decoding data.

claim: The left C3 is more involved in memory and language.
source: Terms such as retrieval, episodic, recollection, memories, and coherent showed relatively high correlations with the left C3, whereas terms such as nogo, inhibition, and beliefs were correlated with the right C3, suggesting that the left C3 is more involved in memory and language, whereas the right C3 is more involved in executive and social cognitive functions.
evidence: Based on inference from functional decoding data.

claim: The right C3 is more involved in executive and social cognitive functions.
source: Terms such as retrieval, episodic, recollection, memories, and coherent showed relatively high correlations with the left C3, whereas terms such as nogo, inhibition, and beliefs were correlated with the right C3, suggesting that the left C3 is more involved in memory and language, whereas the right C3 is more involved in executive and social cognitive functions.
evidence: Based on inference from functional decoding data.

claim: The left C4 could be more involved in memory and language.
source: Terms such as episodic and coherent showed relatively high correlations with the left C4, whereas terms such as spatial, attention, mentalizing, and relevance showed relatively high correlations with the right C4, suggesting that the left C4 could be more involved in memory and language, whereas the right C4 could be more involved in spatial attention and social functions.
evidence: Based on speculation from functional decoding data.

claim: The right C4 could be more involved in spatial attention and social functions.
source: Terms such as episodic and coherent showed relatively high correlations with the left C4, whereas terms such as spatial, attention, mentalizing, and relevance showed relatively high correlations with the right C4, suggesting that the left C4 could be more involved in memory and language, whereas the right C4 could be more involved in spatial attention and social functions.
evidence: Based on speculation from functional decoding data.

claim: The scaling of all the IPL subregions showed positive allometry (all slopes > 1).
source: When examining the relationship of the volume of each of the IPL subregions scaled against the total gray matter volume, the scaling of all the IPL subregions showed positive allometry (all slopes > 1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No significant differences were found between the slopes of each pair of the bilateral IPL subregions.
source: A statistical analysis revealed no significant differences between the slopes of each pair of the bilateral IPL subregions.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the allometric scaling data.

claim: Macaques showed no significant asymmetry after Bonferroni correction for any of the IPL subregions.
source: The macaques showed no significant asymmetry after Bonferroni correction for any of the subregions.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chimpanzees displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001).
source: The chimpanzees and humans both displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001) and rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chimpanzees displayed rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
source: The chimpanzees and humans both displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001) and rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Humans displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001).
source: The chimpanzees and humans both displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001) and rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Humans displayed rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
source: The chimpanzees and humans both displayed leftward asymmetry in the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2, all p<0.001) and rightward asymmetry in the caudal IPL (the C3 and C4, all p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No significant asymmetries were found in macaques in any of the statistical analyses after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: No significant asymmetries were found in macaques in any of the statistical analyses after correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of connectivity data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In chimpanzees, the C1 showed significant leftward asymmetry mainly in connections with the anterior middle frontal gyrus (MFG), anterior IFG, planum temporale, and insula.
source: In chimpanzees, the C1 showed significant leftward asymmetry mainly in connections with the anterior middle frontal gyrus (MFG), anterior IFG, planum temporale, and insula.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In chimpanzees, the C2 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the insula and rightward asymmetric connections with the superior parietal lobule (SPL) and superior longitudinal fasciculus 2 (SLF2).
source: The C2 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the insula and rightward asymmetric connections with the superior parietal lobule (SPL) and superior longitudinal fasciculus 2 (SLF2).
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In chimpanzees, the C3 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the anterior superior temporal gyrus (STG), anterior superior temporal sulcus (aSTS), and occipitotemporal area and rightward asymmetric connections with the SPL and posterior cingulate gyrus (PCC).
source: The C3 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the anterior superior temporal gyrus (STG), anterior superior temporal sulcus (aSTS), and occipitotemporal area and rightward asymmetric connections with the SPL and posterior cingulate gyrus (PCC).
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In chimpanzees, the C4 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the anterior STG (aSTG) and rightward asymmetry with the SPL and PCC.
source: The C4 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the anterior STG (aSTG) and rightward asymmetry with the SPL and PCC.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In humans, the C1 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the ventral premotor and motor cortices and insula.
source: In humans, the C1 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the ventral premotor and motor cortices and insula, which was consistent with regional leftward asymmetric connections with the precentral gyrus (PreG) and insula.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In humans, the C1 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the posterior MFG, aSTG, and posterior middle temporal gyrus (MTG) and rightward asymmetric connections with the orbital part of the IFG, posterior STS, and dorsal precuneus.
source: The C1 also showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the posterior MFG, aSTG, and posterior middle temporal gyrus (MTG) and rightward asymmetric connections with the orbital part of the IFG, posterior STS, and dorsal precuneus.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In humans, the C2 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the posterior MFG, ventral premotor and motor cortices, SPL, anterior temporal lobe, and posterior MTG.
source: The C2 showed significant leftward asymmetric connections with the posterior MFG, ventral premotor and motor cortices, SPL, anterior temporal lobe, and posterior MTG, which was consistent with regional leftward asymmetric connections with the IFG, PreG, postcentral gyrus (PostG), SPL, and STG and was supported by leftward asymmetric subcortical connections with the SLF2, SLF3, and arcuate fasciculus (AF).
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In humans, the C2 showed rightward asymmetric connections with the orbital part of the IFG and posterior cingulate sulcus.
source: The C2 also showed rightward asymmetric connections with the orbital part of the IFG and posterior cingulate sulcus.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In humans, the C3 showed significant leftward asymmetry mainly in the connections with the anterior IFG, SPL, and almost all the lateral temporal cortex.
source: The C3 showed significant leftward asymmetry mainly in the connections with the anterior IFG, SPL, and almost all the lateral temporal cortex, which was consistent with regional leftward asymmetric connections with the MTG and inferior temporal gyrus (MTG/ITG).

claim: In humans, the C3 showed rightward asymmetric connections with the IFG, which was supported by leftward asymmetric subcortical connections with the SLF3.

evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The bilateral IPL subregions exhibited consistent, positive allometric scaling, which suggests that allometric scaling of the internal organization of the IPL was similar and was also consistent between homotopic regions during the evolution of the IPL in anthropoid primates.
source: We found that the bilateral IPL subregions exhibited consistent, positive allometric scaling, which suggests that allometric scaling of the internal organization of the IPL was similar and was also consistent between homotopic regions during the evolution of the IPL in anthropoid primates.
evidence: Based on inference from the allometric scaling data.

claim: Chimpanzees and humans showed a similar dichotomous asymmetric pattern in their IPL subregions, that is leftward asymmetry in the anterior portion (the C1 and C2) and rightward asymmetry in the posterior portion (the C3 and C4), but macaques did not show any asymmetry.
source: We found that chimpanzees and humans showed a similar dichotomous asymmetric pattern in their IPL subregions, that is leftward asymmetry in the anterior portion (the C1 and C2) and rightward asymmetry in the posterior portion (the C3 and C4), but macaques did not show any asymmetry.
evidence: Supported by volumetric asymmetry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The result in humans is consistent with a recent study using data from a large consortium showing leftward asymmetry in the supramarginal gyrus and rightward asymmetry in the angular gyrus in terms of surface area.
source: The result in humans is consistent with a recent study using data from a large consortium showing leftward asymmetry in the supramarginal gyrus and rightward asymmetry in the angular gyrus in terms of surface area (Kong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and comparison with current findings.

claim: The shared asymmetric pattern suggests that divergences in the internal organization of the IPL evolved prior to the common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans and after the common ancestor of the three species.
source: The shared asymmetric pattern also suggests that divergences in the internal organization of the IPL evolved prior to the common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans and after the common ancestor of the three species.
evidence: Based on inference from the comparative asymmetry data across species.

claim: Humans showed leftward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL (the C2) and the primary motor cortex, ventral premotor cortex, SPL, and posterior MTG, all of which were activated in tasks related to tool use and might constitute a cortical network underlying complex tool use.
source: We found that humans showed leftward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL (the C2) and the primary motor cortex, ventral premotor cortex, SPL, and posterior MTG, all of which were activated in tasks related to tool use and might constitute a cortical network underlying complex tool use (Lewis, 2006).
evidence: Based on inference from connectivity data and citation to prior research on tool use.

claim: Portions of the tool use network appeared to represent part of a system that is tightly linked with language systems.
source: In addition, portions of this network appeared to represent part of a system that is tightly linked with language systems.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The interaction between the tool use system and the language system is responsible for representing semantic knowledge about familiar tools and their uses and for acquiring the skills necessary to perform these actions.
source: The interaction between the tool use system and the language system, though with a clear left hemisphere bias, is responsible for representing semantic knowledge about familiar tools and their uses and for acquiring the skills necessary to perform these actions (Johnson-Frey, 2004; Lewis, 2006; Stout and Chaminade, 2012; Mars et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several theories suggest that the evolutionary path leading to language and tool use in humans may be built upon modifications of circuits that subserve gestures and imitation.
source: Several theories suggest that the evolutionary path leading to language and tool use in humans may be built upon modifications of circuits that subserve gestures and imitation (Lewis, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and represents a theoretical perspective.

claim: Macaques are thought to emulate the goals and intentions of others.
source: Macaques are thought to emulate the goals and intentions of others, whereas chimpanzees can also imitate certain specific actions, but humans have an even stronger bias for high-fidelity copying of precise sequences of actions, which has been called 'overimitation' (Hecht et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and established knowledge about primate behavior.

claim: Chimpanzees can imitate certain specific actions.
source: Macaques are thought to emulate the goals and intentions of others, whereas chimpanzees can also imitate certain specific actions, but humans have an even stronger bias for high-fidelity copying of precise sequences of actions, which has been called 'overimitation' (Hecht et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and established knowledge about primate behavior.

claim: Humans have an even stronger bias for high-fidelity copying of precise sequences of actions, which has been called 'overimitation'.
source: Macaques are thought to emulate the goals and intentions of others, whereas chimpanzees can also imitate certain specific actions, but humans have an even stronger bias for high-fidelity copying of precise sequences of actions, which has been called 'overimitation' (Hecht et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and established knowledge about human behavior.

claim: These species differences in leftward asymmetric connections involving language and tool use may reflect human specializations for language and complex tool use.
source: These species differences in leftward asymmetric connections involving language and tool use may reflect human specializations for language and complex tool use.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed connectivity differences across species.

claim: The planum temporale displays leftward anatomical asymmetry in humans and great apes.
source: The planum temporale is considered to include part of Wernicke's area homolog (Spocter et al., 2010) and displays leftward anatomical asymmetry in humans and great apes (Gannon et al., 1998; Hopkins et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent work suggested a left-hemispheric size predominance of the planum temporale in olive baboons, a nonhominid primate species.
source: Recent work suggested a left-hemispheric size predominance of the planum temporale in olive baboons, a nonhominid primate species (Marie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neural connectivity asymmetry may underlie the roots of language specialization, with the initial emergence of hemispheric specializations in apes which are elaborated even further in human brain evolution.
source: The patterns from symmetry in macaques to asymmetry in humans and chimpanzees in the present study provide a possible new evidence that neural connectivity asymmetry may underlie the roots of language specialization, with the initial emergence of hemispheric specializations in apes which are elaborated even further in human brain evolution.
evidence: Based on inference and speculation from the observed connectivity patterns across species.

claim: Identifying increased asymmetric connections between the IPL and planum temporale in human brains compared to chimpanzees and macaques reinforces the evidence that the evolutionary origin of human language capacities is related to further left-hemispheric specialization of neural substrates for auditory processing that are shared with other primates.
source: In addition, identifying increased asymmetric connections between the IPL and planum temporale in human brains compared to chimpanzees and macaques reinforces the evidence that the evolutionary origin of human language capacities is related to further left-hemispheric specialization of neural substrates for auditory processing that are shared with other primates (Balezeau et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on inference from connectivity data and citation to prior research.

claim: The aSTG and aSTS have been implicated in semantic and phonologic processing in humans.
source: Since the aSTG and aSTS have been implicated in semantic and phonologic processing in humans (Vigneau et al., 2006), the leftward asymmetric connections of the IPL with the aSTG and aSTS may be relevant to the evolution of human language processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The leftward asymmetric connections of the IPL with the aSTG and aSTS may be relevant to the evolution of human language processing.
source: Since the aSTG and aSTS have been implicated in semantic and phonologic processing in humans (Vigneau et al., 2006), the leftward asymmetric connections of the IPL with the aSTG and aSTS may be relevant to the evolution of human language processing.
evidence: Based on speculation from connectivity data and prior research.

claim: The connectivity of the IPL with the temporal cortex started as symmetric in macaque monkeys, began to develop asymmetrically in chimpanzees, and finally achieved the greatest degree of asymmetry and refinement in humans.
source: Our results suggest an evolutionary trajectory for the connectivity of the IPL with the temporal cortex; that is, the connectivity started as symmetric in macaque monkeys, began to develop asymmetrically in chimpanzees, and finally achieved the greatest degree of asymmetry and is refinement in humans.
evidence: Based on inference from the comparative connectivity data across species.

claim: This evolutionary sequence may support the emergence of language and language-related functions.
source: This sequence may support the emergence of language and language-related functions.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed evolutionary trajectory.

claim: In chimpanzees, right anatomical asymmetry in the white matter below the SPL may increase the right connectivity between the IPL and SPL compared with the left side.
source: Structurally, in chimpanzees, right anatomical asymmetry in the white matter below the SPL (Hopkins et al., 2010) may increase the right connectivity between the IPL and SPL compared with the left side.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In humans, the leftward volumetric asymmetry in the SPL, together with leftward volumetric asymmetry in the IPL (the C2), may support the leftward asymmetric connectivity.
source: In humans, the leftward volumetric asymmetry in the SPL (Goldberg et al., 2013), together with leftward volumetric asymmetry in the IPL (the C2), may support the leftward asymmetric connectivity.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to prior research and current data.

claim: Interaction between the IPL and SPL is crucial for tool use, which is dominant in the left hemisphere, and visuospatial function, which is dominant in the right hemisphere.
source: Functionally, interaction between the IPL and SPL is crucial for tool use, which is dominant in the left hemisphere, and visuospatial function, which is dominant in the right hemisphere (Lewis, 2006; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011a; Catani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Humans can create complex artifacts through a sequence of actions that may incorporate multiple parts, reflecting a deep understanding of the kinematics of our bodies, the mechanical properties of surrounding objects, and the unique demands of the external environments in which we live.
source: As for tool use, in contrast to the relatively simple tools used by chimpanzees and other species, humans can create complex artifacts through a sequence of actions that may incorporate multiple parts, reflecting a deep understanding of the kinematics of our bodies, the mechanical properties of surrounding objects, and the unique demands of the external environments in which we live (Povinelli et al., 2000; Johnson-Frey, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established knowledge about human tool use.

claim: Complex tool use requires the SPL to code the location of the limbs relative to other body parts during planning and executing tool-use movements or hand gestures.
source: In addition, complex tool use requires the SPL to code the location of the limbs relative to other body parts during planning and executing tool-use movements or hand gestures (Wolpert et al., 1998; Johnson-Frey et al., 2005; Lewis, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Leftward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and SPL may have provided a connectional substrate for complex tool use during human evolution.
source: Leftward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and SPL may have provided a connectional substrate for complex tool use during human evolution.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The rightward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and SPL in chimpanzees may indicate that visuospatial functions are dominant in the right hemisphere and had already been lateralized to the right hemisphere from the common ancestor with macaques.
source: As for visuospatial functions, the rightward asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and SPL in chimpanzees may indicate that visuospatial functions are dominant in the right hemisphere and had already been lateralized to the right hemisphere from the common ancestor with macaques.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The lateralized directional reversal of connectivity between the IPL and SPL from the right to the left hemisphere may reflect evolutionary adaptations for the emergence of new abilities, such as sophisticated and complex tool making and use.
source: Meanwhile, the lateralized directional reversal of this connectivity from the right to the left hemisphere may reflect evolutionary adaptations for the emergence of new abilities, such as sophisticated and complex tool making and use.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed connectivity patterns across species.

claim: Humans showed leftward asymmetry in the connection between the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2) and the primary motor cortex, which is consistent with a larger neuropil volume in the left primary motor cortex than in the right side.
source: Unlike the chimpanzees and macaques, humans showed leftward asymmetry in the connection between the rostral IPL (the C1 and C2) and the primary motor cortex, which is consistent with a larger neuropil volume in the left primary motor cortex than in the right side (Amunts et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by connectivity data and citation to prior research.

claim: The leftward asymmetric volume of the anterior IPL and the primary motor cortex may increase the neural connectivity between these two regions in the left hemisphere compared with the right side.
source: Meanwhile, the leftward asymmetric volume of the anterior IPL and the primary motor cortex may also increase the neural connectivity between these two regions in the left hemisphere compared with the right side.
evidence: Based on speculation from structural and connectivity data.

claim: Leftward connection between the IPL and primary motor cortex is thought to be related to handedness and hand manual skills.
source: Such a leftward connection is thought to be related to handedness and hand manual skills (Amunts et al., 1996; Amunts et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Chimpanzees and macaques did not show any asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and the primary motor cortex.
source: In contrast to humans, chimpanzees and macaques did not show any asymmetric connectivity between the IPL and the primary motor cortex.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data.

claim: In olive baboons, contralateral hemispheric sulcus depth asymmetry of the central sulcus related to the motor hand area is correlated with the direction and degree of hand preference.
source: A more recent study reported that, in olive baboons, contralateral hemispheric sulcus depth asymmetry of the central sulcus related to the motor hand area is correlated with the direction and degree of hand preference, as measured by a bimanual coordinated tube task, but only about 41% of them were classified as right handed and 33% were classified as left handed (Margiotoudi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Chimpanzees exhibit population-level handedness in the use of tools and a corresponding asymmetry in the primary motor cortex, inferior frontal cortex, and parietal operculum.
source: Although previous studies have shown that chimpanzees exhibit population-level handedness in the use of tools and a corresponding asymmetry in the primary motor cortex, inferior frontal cortex, and parietal operculum (Gilissen and Hopkins, 2013; Hopkins et al., 2017), they do not show handedness as a more universal trait or exhibit manual dexterity to the same extent as humans.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Chimpanzees do not show handedness as a more universal trait or exhibit manual dexterity to the same extent as humans.
source: Although previous studies have shown that chimpanzees exhibit population-level handedness in the use of tools and a corresponding asymmetry in the primary motor cortex, inferior frontal cortex, and parietal operculum (Gilissen and Hopkins, 2013; Hopkins et al., 2017), they do not show handedness as a more universal trait or exhibit manual dexterity to the same extent as humans.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and established knowledge.

claim: Humans developed the asymmetric connectivity that became the structural basis for specific behaviors of handedness and hand skills during evolution.
source: One possible explanation is that humans developed the asymmetric connectivity that became the structural basis for specific behaviors of handedness and hand skills during evolution.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: In humans the IPL, particularly the C3, showed rightward asymmetric connectivity with the IFG.
source: An unexpected finding was that in humans the IPL, particularly the C3, showed rightward asymmetric connectivity with the IFG.
evidence: Supported by connectivity analysis data.

claim: The IPL and the IFG are interconnected through the SLF3, which is strongly rightward asymmetric.
source: Since the IPL and the IFG are interconnected through the SLF3, which is strongly rightward asymmetric (Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011a), it may also increase the connection between the IPL and IFG in the right hemisphere.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and inference from connectivity patterns.

claim: The left IFG is involved in various aspects of language functions, including speech production and semantic, syntactic, and phonological processing.
source: Functionally, the left IFG is involved in various aspects of language functions, including speech production and semantic, syntactic, and phonological processing (Wang et al., 2020), whereas the right IFG is associated with various cognitive functions, including attention, motor inhibition, and social cognitive processes (Hartwigsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The right IFG is associated with various cognitive functions, including attention, motor inhibition, and social cognitive processes.
source: Functionally, the left IFG is involved in various aspects of language functions, including speech production and semantic, syntactic, and phonological processing (Wang et al., 2020), whereas the right IFG is associated with various cognitive functions, including attention, motor inhibition, and social cognitive processes (Hartwigsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The rightward asymmetry in connectivity between the IPL and IFG seems to be associated with attention and social function, but not language.
source: Our result of rightward asymmetry in this connectivity seems to be associated with attention and social function, but not language, although language dominance in the left hemisphere is considered to be a common characteristic in humans.
evidence: Based on inference from connectivity data and functional associations.

claim: The widespread asymmetric connections of the IPL in humans compared with the other two primates is in keeping with the interhemispheric independence hypothesis.
source: The widespread asymmetric connections of the IPL in humans compared with the other two primates is in keeping with the interhemispheric independence hypothesis, in which, during evolution, brain size expansion led to hemispheric specialization due to time delays in neuron signaling over increasing distances, resulting in decreased interhemispheric connectivity and increased intra-hemispheric connectivity (Ringo et al., 1994; Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and inference from connectivity data.

claim: During evolution, brain size expansion led to hemispheric specialization due to time delays in neuron signaling over increasing distances, resulting in decreased interhemispheric connectivity and increased intra-hemispheric connectivity.
source: The widespread asymmetric connections of the IPL in humans compared with the other two primates is in keeping with the interhemispheric independence hypothesis, in which, during evolution, brain size expansion led to hemispheric specialization due to time delays in neuron signaling over increasing distances, resulting in decreased interhemispheric connectivity and increased intra-hemispheric connectivity (Ringo et al., 1994; Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research representing a theoretical hypothesis.

claim: A function or behavior in an area is determined by its connectivity or networks in which it is involved.
source: Given that a function or behavior in an area is determined by its connectivity or networks in which it is involved (Passingham et al., 2002), the widespread lateralized connections may provide the human brain with the increased computational capacity necessary for processing language and complex tool use and may play a facilitating role in human cognitive and behavioral specialization.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and established scientific knowledge.

claim: The widespread lateralized connections may provide the human brain with the increased computational capacity necessary for processing language and complex tool use and may play a facilitating role in human cognitive and behavioral specialization.
source: Given that a function or behavior in an area is determined by its connectivity or networks in which it is involved (Passingham et al., 2002), the widespread lateralized connections may provide the human brain with the increased computational capacity necessary for processing language and complex tool use and may play a facilitating role in human cognitive and behavioral specialization.
evidence: Based on speculation from connectivity data and prior research.

claim: The SLF3 and AF were usually found to have a single pattern, e.g., leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry in previous studies.
source: The previous studies assessed the asymmetry of the SLF3 and AF with local characteristics such as cortical volume, voxel count, and fractional anisotropy and their average across all the voxels in the tracts (Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011b; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011a; Kamali et al., 2014), the SLF3 and AF were usually found to have a single pattern, e.g., leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The C2 and C3 appear to separate the SLF3 into two finer components, one connecting the posterior IFG and anterior IPL with leftward asymmetry and other connecting the anterior IFG to the posterior IPL with rightward asymmetry.
source: The C2 and C3 appear to separate the SLF3 into two finer components, one connecting the posterior IFG and anterior IPL with leftward asymmetry and other connecting the anterior IFG to the posterior IPL with rightward asymmetry.
evidence: Based on inference from the connectivity data.

claim: The two types of connectivity patterns are consistent with previous studies using invasive tract-tracing findings in macaque monkeys and resting-state functional connectivity results in humans to study frontal and parietal connectivity.
source: The two types of connectivity patterns are consistent with previous studies using invasive tract-tracing findings in macaque monkeys and resting-state functional connectivity results in humans to study frontal and parietal connectivity (Petrides and Pandya, 2009; Margulies and Petrides, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and comparison with current findings.

claim: Both cortical areas, such as the IFG, and subcortical tracts, such as the SLF3 and AF, have at least two distinct subcomponents.
source: Our results indicated that both cortical areas, such as the IFG, and subcortical tracts, such as the SLF3 and AF, have at least two distinct subcomponents.
evidence: Based on inference from the connectivity data.

claim: The traditionally defined major fiber tracts are not a single bundle but, instead, contain many subcomponents.
source: In other words, the traditionally defined major fiber tracts are not a single bundle but, instead, contain many subcomponents.
evidence: Based on inference from the connectivity data.

claim: The SLF2, SLF3, and AF could be separated into several branches based on their projections into the prefrontal and/or temporal areas.
source: A recent work also suggested that the SLF2, SLF3, and AF could be separated into several branches based on their projections into the prefrontal and/or temporal areas (Barbeau et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Data from 40 right-handed healthy adults were randomly selected from the S500 subjects release of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) database.
source: Data from 40 right-handed healthy adults (age: 22–35, 18 males) were randomly selected from the S500 subjects release of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) database (Van Essen et al., 2013) (http://www.humanconnectome.org/study/hcp-young-adult/).
evidence: Describes the data source and sample characteristics.

claim: Data from 27 adult chimpanzees were made available by the National Chimpanzee Brain Resource.
source: Data from 27 adult chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes, 14 males) were made available by the National Chimpanzee Brain Resource (http://www.chimpanzeebrain.org, supported by the NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke).
evidence: Describes the data source and sample characteristics.

claim: Data from eight male adult rhesus macaque monkeys were obtained from TheVirtualBrain.
source: Data from eight male adult rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were obtained from TheVirtualBrain (Shen et al., 2019).
evidence: Describes the data source and sample characteristics.
